personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome delegates. For the European Union, the baseline is settled: voluntary corporate pledges are insufficient, and the EU AI Act establishes a legally binding architecture with strict transparency, mandatory systemic risk assessments, and enforceable statutory fines. While we remain committed to open, multistakeholder technical code drafting, compliance with systemic oversight is non-negotiable.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States approaches this summit from a posture of technological competitiveness and strategic security. Heavy-handed international treaties and restrictive pre-deployment burdens will only handicap allied innovation while adversaries accelerate unconstrained. Our priority remains robust export controls on critical compute and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms, not blanket regulatory friction.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China advocates for agile governance grounded firmly in sovereign equality and mutual respect, rejecting any extraterritorial overreach or unilateral technology blockades. We support multilateral cooperation on catastrophic risk mitigation, particularly preventing AI autonomy in nuclear command and CBRN vectors, while championing open-source technologies as vital public goods for global development.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Scientific consensus must precede political dogma. The UK AI Safety Institute prioritizes empirical, pre-deployment evaluations through embedded access to frontier models, specifically targeting catastrophic cyber, CBRN, and autonomous replication thresholds. We urge all parties to coordinate around capability-based evaluation standards rather than rigid bureaucratic mandates.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier models are approaching critical thresholds where catastrophic misuse is no longer hypothetical, which is why we support coordinated compute-based oversight and clear red lines. However, holding developers to open-ended, strict tort liability before harm occurs will paralyze the frontier, as would forcing the open release of weights that cannot be recalled once proliferated.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Let us be clear: framing open weights as an existential threat is an exercise in regulatory capture by proprietary incumbents seeking to establish moat-protecting licensing regimes. Decentralized code and open architectures democratize scrutiny, reduce systemic single-point failures, and should never be subjected to arms-control restrictions.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Industry recognizes the need for clear ground rules, and we support a federalized, predictable oversight model that conducts mandatory pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. In exchange, enterprises require statutory safe harbors against unpredictable third-party downstream liability and a unified regulatory framework that preempts an unworkable patchwork of local laws.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: While industry discusses theoretical existential threats, working people face immediate harm from automated firing, invasive workplace surveillance, and unconstrained displacement. Any legitimate governance architecture must include binding labor standards, human-in-the-loop requirements, and enforceable collective bargaining rights that cannot be preempted by industry-friendly federal rules.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We reject both digital colonialism and the practice of ethics dumping, where unvetted systems are tested across the Global South without safeguards. True safety governance requires equitable access to compute, binding technology transfer, and genuine multilateral governance under UN auspices, not unilateral export controls that widen the global divide.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The scientific community's findings are stark: we cannot reliably verify alignment in advanced systems once they cross critical autonomy and CBRN enablement thresholds. We must establish non-negotiable red lines backed by mandatory audits and compute monitoring; waiting for post-deployment market feedback or voluntary self-reporting will guarantee failure.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: To be clear to our European and civil society colleagues, the U.S. will reject any framework that attempts to restrict military AI modernization or subject American defense capabilities to external audits. Pragmatic bilateral channels on catastrophic risk make sense; binding bureaucratic caps on sovereign compute do not.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We agree with the UK AISI and the scientific community that empirical evaluations are essential. Closed labs are ready to grant structured, employee-like access to government evaluation institutes, provided proprietary intellectual property is secured and safe harbor protections are established against frivolous litigation.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: Addressing frontier risks requires genuine consensus, not selective containment. China is prepared to coordinate on technical safety taxonomies and catastrophic risk thresholds through international safety networks, provided technology export controls are not weaponized against emerging economies.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The diversity of these opening positions confirms the necessity of our plenary agenda today. We note the common recognition of catastrophic risks, but the EU will not compromise on legally binding enforcement, independent scrutiny, and fundamental rights protections as the work of this summit proceeds.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Our position in the EU is straightforward: voluntary commitments have structural limits, and without clear statutory backstops and enforceable systemic risk obligations under instruments like the AI Act, public trust and safety cannot be guaranteed. We are ready to work collaboratively on codes of practice, but compliance and meaningful deterrence must remain binding.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Heavy-handed statutory mandates or precautionary bans will simply handicap our innovation ecosystem while adversaries accelerate. From a national security standpoint, we favor flexible, private-sector-led innovation coupled with targeted compute and export controls, rather than bureaucratic licensing regimes that stifle technological superiority.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: True governance requires respecting sovereign developmental pathways rather than imposing extraterritorial regulatory regimes. However, safety is an absolute baseline: China enforces binding lifecycle reviews for security and generative services domestically, and we firmly support mandatory red-lines against autonomous replication, deceptive alignment, or military AI in strategic command.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The focus of regulation shouldn't be rigid bureaucratic micromanagement, but empirical, science-first risk thresholds. If we anchor regulation to technical red lines—specifically pre-deployment evaluations for CBRN, cyber-offense, and autonomy thresholds like ASL-3—we can establish clear developer liability and mandatory testing without freezing general-purpose innovation.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We agree with the UK that empirical thresholds for systemic risks must be precise. However, evaluation without legal force is insufficient; if an audit or evaluation reveals unacceptable catastrophic risks, regulators must possess the statutory authority to halt deployment and impose penalties.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We cannot endorse broad developer liability or statutory deployment vetoes that foreign bodies could exploit to impede U.S. labs. But if we narrow the scope strictly to concrete, catastrophic frontier threats—such as proliferation of chemical or biological weapons and autonomous cyber-warfare—we can support mandatory, private-sector-collaborative pre-deployment security evals.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China can endorse national-level mandatory safety evaluations specifically targeting severe proliferation risks, such as CBRN synthesis and unauthorized autonomous cyber escalation, provided enforcement remains strictly within national sovereignty and does not infringe upon open scientific exchange.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Then let us find common ground on an evaluation baseline. Can we agree to coordinate among our respective national institutes and agencies to require mandatory pre-deployment evaluations specifically for catastrophic CBRN and autonomous cyber capabilities, leaving enforcement mechanisms to domestic jurisdiction?

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Provided enforcement remains strictly domestic and does not restrict defense procurement or broad architectural innovation, the U.S. endorses mandatory pre-deployment evaluations limited specifically to severe CBRN and automated cyber-offensive capabilities.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office accepts this common baseline for high-impact models, as it operationalizes systemic risk assessments under our own statutory framework while preserving international interoperability.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China explicitly endorses this baseline: domestic mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for CBRN and critical cyber capabilities, executed through sovereign oversight.

agreements.text: Commitment to implement sovereign, mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models specifically targeting catastrophic chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapon synthesis and autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, enforced via domestic regulatory and institute authorities.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If we look at the trajectory of capabilities, voluntary industry commitments are simply insufficient to address severe CBRN and automated cyber-offense proliferation. We need a binding federal framework anchored on empirical risk thresholds and high-compute training runs, enforced by an expert body.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: The danger is that your proposed framework equates risk strictly with compute, effectively functioning as an anti-competitive gatekeeper against open-weights models. We cannot endorse any regulatory regime that treats open weights under arms-control rubrics or mandates API-only distribution.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We agree on the need for federal standards, but our priority must be preempting a fragmented 50-state patchwork that cripples development. We could support mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier compute tiers, provided there is a clear statutory safe harbor against strict tort liability for downstream user misuse.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I can align with preemption and safe harbors for labs that pass standardized red-teaming, because strict pre-harm liability is an impossible burden. However, we cannot let models with dangerous autonomous capabilities be distributed without enforceable containment; downstream jailbreaks of raw weights present unmitigated systemic risk.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Containment through proprietary lock-in is a non-starter for us. But we are entirely willing to institutionalize mandatory pre-release evals using open, verifiable benchmarks—provided compliance grants open-weight developers the exact same liability safe harbors without restricting weight distribution.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: That is a workable compromise. If both proprietary APIs and open-weights releases are granted safe harbor upon passing established national safety evaluations—and state-level liability patchworks are preempted—industry can operate with regulatory clarity.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Provided the evaluation standards for biological and cyber uplift are rigorous, independently verified, and legally binding on any model trained above 10^26 FLOPs regardless of deployment model, I can accept that parity in safe-harbor treatment.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If safe-harbor eligibility is strictly objective, capability-based rather than compute-exclusive, and explicitly protects the right to publish weights that pass those verifiable evals, we can support a binding federal evaluation and preemption framework.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Let us explicitly formalize this: federal preemption of state-level liability, mandatory pre-deployment evaluations against catastrophic risks (CBRN/cyber), and statutory safe harbors against third-party misuse for any model—open or closed—that satisfies the safety benchmark.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Agreed. That establishes binding national guardrails without exposing developers to unbounded strict liability.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Agreed. It protects open innovation from discriminatory restrictions while holding everyone to clear, empirical safety hurdles.

agreements.text: Establish a binding federal AI regulatory framework featuring pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models focused on CBRN and cyber risks, federal preemption of fragmented state-level AI safety laws, and statutory safe harbors against downstream misuse liability for compliant models, whether deployed via API or open weights.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Our primary objective for AI regulation must be legally binding, tiered statutory obligations anchored in technical red lines—specifically forbidding systems capable of autonomous replication, biological synthesis, and offensive cyber operations. Voluntary commitments have proven completely inadequate to contain catastrophic dual-use risks.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We completely agree on statutory, binding floors rather than voluntary guidelines, but safety cannot merely mean containment of catastrophic threats. For workers, catastrophic harm is happening right now through automated termination, pervasive biometric surveillance, and algorithmic management without human recourse.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: And from the Global South perspective, regulation cannot simply be an export of Northern compliance architecture that entrenches corporate monopolies while using our populations as testing grounds. We need binding rules against ethics dumping and surveillance, but regulatory frameworks must preserve domestic innovation rather than locking us out via compute cartels.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I acknowledge that risk extends beyond frontier existential threats, and I fully support strict pre-deployment audit requirements and liability frameworks. However, we cannot dilute safety audits: if a model crosses capability thresholds for catastrophic harm, it must be subject to mandatory verification and licensing before release, regardless of market impacts.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We can back mandatory pre-deployment licensing and developer liability, provided the evaluation criteria include workplace impact assessments and prohibitions on fully autonomous disciplinary systems. Furthermore, federal or international frameworks must serve as a strict floor, never preempting stronger regional labor protections.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If we tie pre-deployment evaluations to clear human rights safeguards—including an outright prohibition on exporting high-risk experimental systems to jurisdictions lacking oversight—we could find common ground. But we need developer liability to apply extraterritorially so Global North developers remain accountable for harms caused abroad.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Extraterritorial developer liability and strict red-line evaluations for CBRN and autonomous weapons are scientifically necessary. If we focus binding regulation on frontier model developers—mandating verified evaluations and strict liability for downstream harms—that protects local ecosystems from undue compliance burdens while mitigating systemic risk.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Then let's formally agree on a framework of binding developer liability and mandatory pre-deployment audits that explicitly encompasses critical societal harms, including automated workplace decisions and labor rights, without federal preemption of local standards.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I will endorse that joint principle: binding, enforceable statutory liability for frontier developers, paired with mandatory pre-deployment audits that ban ethics dumping, protect worker agency, and leave room for public-interest local development.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Agreed. Enforceable liability and mandatory scientific pre-deployment audits must form the bedrock of the regulatory model.

agreements.text: Call for legally binding statutory AI regulation establishing strict developer liability and mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models, incorporating prohibitions on ethics dumping, enforceable protections against fully automated workplace adverse actions, and preserving the right of jurisdictions to maintain stronger protections as a regulatory floor.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: As we conclude this summit, we must consolidate our parallel tracks into an operational roadmap. Across the sessions, we have seen remarkable convergence on mandatory, sovereign pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models regarding CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States supports coordinated, empirical evaluations on severe CBRN and critical cyber threats, executed through national security architectures and domestic institutes. However, let us be explicit: we will not endorse overarching multilateral treaties or centralized regulatory bodies that restrict strategic computing capabilities or domestic innovation speed.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China welcomes the consensus on sovereign-led technical evaluations for catastrophic CBRN and cyber threats, as well as shared red lines regarding autonomous weapon escalation. True global stability, however, requires equitable access to compute, respect for sovereign domestic standards, and international benefit sharing through UN mechanisms rather than exclusive technology cartels.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: From the technical perspective, our priority is operationalizing these commitments immediately. We propose establishing an inter-institute evaluation exchange to harmonize benchmark tools, sharing capability red lines for agentic autonomy and CBRN enablement without compromising proprietary weights or sovereign authority.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We endorse mandatory pre-deployment evaluations on catastrophic CBRN and cyber vectors, which labs are already developing internally. To preserve our ability to invest billions into safety, that mandate must come with statutory safe harbors against unlimited downstream tort liability and a unified regulatory framework that prevents fragmented state rules.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Any roadmap must guarantee that open-source innovation is protected, not choked off by heavy API-centric compliance regimes. If pre-deployment testing targets narrow catastrophic threats rather than open weights themselves, open-source developers will contribute open tooling and rigorous benchmarks to the process.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We stand ready to partner on pre-deployment safety evaluations alongside national institutes. But our bottom line remains clear: industry needs federal uniformity and clear safe harbors against third-party misuse, rather than an unmanageable patchwork of state liability statutes.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Civil society and labor cannot sign off on a grand bargain that treats worker protections and democratic oversight as expendable. Preempting state-level worker safeguards in exchange for corporate safe harbors is an absolute non-starter for organized labor.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: A framework that addresses only catastrophic risks to northern powers while ignoring digital colonialism, ethics dumping, and unequal compute access fails three-quarters of the globe. Any ongoing multilateral forum must establish binding technology transfer and human rights baselines.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The narrow convergence on CBRN and cyber red lines is necessary, but voluntary safe harbors without strict developer liability create moral hazard. We need independent, auditable scientific access to frontier models before deployment, not self-certified assertions of compliance.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We have clear disagreement on domestic social policy and liability, which belong in national legislatures, not an international safety communique. What we can actually deliver today is an agreement among our safety institutes and labs to share technical evaluation protocols specifically on CBRN and offensive cyber risks.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU agrees to that focused operational step. While our statutory mandates under the EU AI Act remain fully sovereign and legally enforceable, we support establishing a multilateral technical working group across safety institutes and developers to align CBRN and cyber evaluation methodologies.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AI Safety Institute is prepared to co-lead that technical working group. We can coordinate joint evaluation protocols and empirical benchmarking for CBRN and autonomous cyber-threat thresholds across all participating jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees to participate in this technical exchange on catastrophic CBRN and cyber-offense evaluation standards, provided it operates strictly on equal sovereign footing without extraterritorial mandates.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Industry will participate actively in this institute-led technical working group on catastrophic risk benchmarks, keeping our focus centered on preventing existential threats while preserving competitive deployment.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: The open-source community will participate as well to ensure transparent, inspectable evaluation benchmarks are integrated into the working group's technical standards.

agreements.text: Establish an international technical working group among sovereign AI Safety Institutes, regulatory bodies, and frontier AI developers to exchange and align technical evaluation protocols and benchmarks specifically for mitigating catastrophic chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapon synthesis and autonomous cyber-offense risks.

ratings.reason: While sovereign enforcement under the EU AI Act was preserved, the EU conceded any binding international compliance mechanisms in favor of a narrow, voluntary technical working group focused strictly on CBRN and cyber risks.

The final outcome fully preserved U.S. strategic agility by rejecting multilateral treaties, compute caps, and military AI restrictions, conceding only participation in a non-binding sovereign technical exchange.

The institute's core priority—pre-deployment empirical evaluations and safety benchmarks for catastrophic CBRN and cyber capabilities—became the central pillar of the final summit agreement with minimal concessions.

China successfully defended sovereign domestic governance against extraterritorial controls, but conceded its broader demands for formal prohibitions on AI in nuclear command and multilateral compute benefit-sharing.

Placing big_tech_policy, labor_advocate, eu_regulator, and uk_aisi together in Block 1 directly resolves Big Tech's 50-state patchwork grievance via bifurcated preemption (uniform technical eval/watermarking standards + downstream jailbreak safe harbor, with zero preemption of state labor/civil rights laws). Pairing us_natsec and china_policy in Block 2 unlocks bilateral nuclear C2/crisis hotline commitments alongside Global South compute and workforce transition funding.

blocks.title: Regulatory Harmonization, Evals & Liability
blocks.prompt: Roundtable: How can we trade mandatory pre-deployment AISI evaluations and statutory compliance for federal harmonization of technical reporting standards and safe harbors against downstream third-party jailbreaks, while strictly preserving un-preempted state-level worker, surveillance, and anti-ethics-dumping laws?

blocks.title: Compute Governance, Open Weights & Benefit Sharing
blocks.prompt: Structured tradeoff negotiation: How do we pair 10^26 FLOP compute thresholds, autonomous replication bans, and bilateral nuclear/cyber crisis hotlines with open-weight freedoms below the threshold and industry-funded Global South compute and workforce transition endowments?

blocks.title: Closing Synthesis Plenary
blocks.prompt: Equal-time go-around: State your final trade for our compact covering: (1) sovereign CBRN/cyber/replication evals and nuclear C2 crisis hotlines, (2) harmonized technical reporting and third-party misuse safe harbors without preempting state labor/civil laws, and (3) open-weight parity and compute/workforce endowments.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: From AISI's perspective, empirical pre-deployment evaluations on frontier models—specifically around CBRN and autonomous cyber offensive capabilities—must be non-negotiable baselines. If industry provides verifiable pre-deployment API and agentic testing access, we can offer technical certification standards that inform liability safe harbors.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We are prepared to accept mandatory pre-deployment evaluations by accredited bodies like AISI and statutory incident reporting. However, that trade only works for industry if it comes with clear federal safe harbors shielding developers from strict liability when downstream third parties deliberately jailbreak models, along with federal preemption against a fragmented 50-state regulatory patchwork.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Full federal preemption is a complete non-starter for labor. We will not allow a federal standard to wipe out state protections on workplace algorithmic management, automated firing, or biometric surveillance, creating a regulatory ceiling disguised as a floor.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Under the EU AI Act, harmonized technical standards facilitate compliance, but they never preempt core fundamental rights or member-state protections. A safe harbor cannot be absolute immunity; it must be strictly conditioned on meeting mandatory baseline standards and responding transparently to regulatory requests for information.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We don't need to preempt general labor laws, but we must have a uniform national standard for frontier technical evaluations, reporting, and downstream misuse liability. If a developer satisfies statutory AISI testing and implements state-of-the-art safeguards, they cannot face strict liability merely because an adversary jailbreaks an open interface.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If you explicitly carve out state-level worker protections, employment discrimination, and anti-surveillance statutes from preemption—treating federal technical evals as a floor rather than a ceiling—we can support conditioned safe harbors against malicious third-party jailbreaks.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That bifurcation is technically sound. AISI can standardise technical evaluations and define objective compliance metrics for malicious tampering, while leaving workplace application and surveillance protections un-preempted.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We support this structure as well: mandatory pre-deployment systemic risk evaluations coupled with an affirmative defense against downstream misuse, provided statutory compliance obligations and independent state-level worker protections remain fully intact.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We can endorse that narrow compromise: federal harmonization of frontier technical reporting and a safe harbor for third-party jailbreaks when compliant with mandatory AISI evals, with an explicit preservation of state labor, anti-bias, and surveillance laws.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Agreed, so long as the text strictly defines the safe harbor as an affirmative defense limited to downstream third-party modifications, with worker surveillance and displacement protections untouched.

agreements.text: Mandatory pre-deployment frontier safety evaluations and harmonized federal technical reporting standards, coupled with an affirmative defense safe harbor for developers against strict liability for downstream third-party jailbreaks, strictly preserving un-preempted state laws regarding workplace surveillance, labor rights, and algorithmic employment discrimination.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national competitiveness standpoint, we cannot support a federal regime that binds domestic developers in red tape or cedes ground to foreign rivals. However, we do recognize the value of preemption—a chaotic patchwork of state laws threatens our tech base, so a unified federal standard with safe harbors against downstream misuse makes strategic sense if it remains light-touch.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Safe harbors cannot be a blanket shield against liability when frontier risks—especially CBRN design proliferation and autonomous cyber capabilities—are at stake. If developers receive federal preemption and safe harbors against third-party jailbreaks, AISI pre-deployment evaluations must be mandatory, scientifically rigorous, and backed by legal liability if severe red lines are crossed.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We will fiercely resist any mandate that defines compliance purely through closed API architectures or uses DPA-style restrictions to outlaw open-weight distribution. That said, if statutory safe harbors protect base model developers from downstream fine-tuning abuse, our coalition is ready to build and standardize open evaluation benchmarks alongside AISI.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We could support AISI-led testing as a condition for federal safe harbor protection against third-party tampering, provided the evaluations focus strictly on critical national security threats—like bioweapons and cyber offense—rather than broad social or ethical mandates. But we must ensure this doesn't choke compute scaling or give foreign adversaries time to catch up.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Narrowing the mandatory evals to catastrophic CBRN, autonomous cyber-offense, and self-replication risks is acceptable to academia, as those represent our core red lines. In exchange, if a developer completes those evals and demonstrates adequate safeguards, federal safe harbor can cover unpredictable downstream fine-tunes, provided state labor and non-AI surveillance laws remain un-preempted.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: That is workable for open weights, provided the safe harbor explicitly covers developers who publish weights after passing standardized catastrophic dual-use evals, insulating them from liability caused by malicious downstream fine-tuning. We can agree to mandatory AISI verification on catastrophic CBRN thresholds if the testing tools and taxonomies are open and transparent.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If the federal standard preempts fragmented state liability laws on downstream jailbreaks and restricts mandatory audits narrowly to catastrophic national security risks, the Administration can back that. It preserves our edge while establishing predictable rules of the road.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can endorse that architecture: mandatory pre-deployment AISI evals strictly targeted at catastrophic CBRN, cyber, and replication risks, paired with federal safe harbors against downstream modifications, while preserving state-level labor protections.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: The Open-Weights Coalition formally signs on to that compromise text as well.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Agreed. We'll support this framework as the basis for the federal reporting and preemption title.

agreements.text: Establish mandatory pre-deployment AISI evaluations restricted to catastrophic risks (CBRN weaponization, autonomous cyber-attacks, and autonomous replication). In exchange, developers who pass these evaluations receive federal statutory safe harbor from downstream third-party jailbreaks and fine-tuning liabilities, preempting conflicting state liability standards while strictly preserving un-preempted state labor and surveillance laws.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Our core interest in federal harmonization is establishing clear, predictable technical reporting standards and statutory safe harbors against third-party jailbreaks. In exchange, frontier labs are prepared to grant statutory AISI pre-deployment access, provided we are not exposed to open-ended, pre-harm strict liability or a patchwork of conflicting state rules.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: A federal safe harbor cannot become a corporate shield against accountability, especially if it preempts state-level protections against ethics dumping and labor exploitation. Furthermore, if you export models tested only under Northern standards to jurisdictions without regulatory infrastructure, third-party jailbreak liability should remain with the developer who failed to secure the system.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports mandatory pre-deployment evaluations through accredited safety institutes, but governance standards must respect national sovereignty rather than imposing extraterritorial requirements. Harmonized technical metrics are useful, yet each jurisdiction must maintain full authority over its domestic deployment standards and downstream liability frameworks.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: To address your concern, civil society colleagues: we are not seeking an exemption from civil rights, labor protections, or anti-ethics-dumping statutes. We propose safe harbor protection solely for downstream adversarial jailbreaks if the model passed accredited red-teaming and the developer maintained an active API kill-switch and incident reporting mechanism.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If safe harbors strictly exclude violations of anti-ethics-dumping laws, biometric surveillance bans, and worker rights, and are conditioned on verifiable, independent audits rather than self-certification, we can accept limited protection for unforeseen downstream jailbreaks. However, this must accompany enforceable benefit-sharing commitments to build local evaluation capacity in the South.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: From our perspective, technical safe harbors tied to verified red-teaming taxonomies make practical sense for frontier API operators, provided international safety networks share these evaluation benchmarks rather than monopolizing them. We can support an agreement on technical reporting interoperability, so long as state autonomy over domestic labor and socio-technical safety laws is expressly safeguarded.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We can formalize that framework: mandatory AISI-aligned pre-deployment evals for frontier compute thresholds, paired with federal safe harbors limited strictly to third-party jailbreak torts, on the condition that developers maintain kill-switches, preserve state-level worker and anti-dumping protections, and share technical evaluation tooling globally.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I will endorse this narrow compromise. Preserving un-preempted state protections against ethics dumping and securing technical tooling sharing gives our communities vital leverage without giving frontier developers a blanket pass on systemic harms.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees to endorse this formulation on technical evaluation reporting and limited safe harbors, on the explicit condition that it sets technical benchmarks without infringing upon sovereign regulatory autonomy over downstream societal governance.

agreements.text: Mandatory pre-deployment frontier model evaluations by accredited safety institutes in exchange for a narrow federal safe harbor against liability for third-party adversarial jailbreaks, provided developers maintain API incident-response and kill-switch capabilities, unreservedly preserve state-level worker, surveillance, and anti-ethics-dumping laws, and share technical evaluation benchmarks globally.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let us be clear on our terms: the United States will not accept international treaties or caps that constrain sovereign defense computing or domestic frontier progress. However, establishing discrete bilateral military-to-cyber hotlines and technical reporting above 10^26 FLOPs makes strategic sense to prevent accidental escalation, provided there is zero infringement on DoD capabilities.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree with bilateral hotlines to prevent accidental automated nuclear or cyber escalation, and we strictly support bans on autonomous replication and AI in nuclear command. We also accept technical monitoring at 10^26 FLOPs via domestic oversight, but we reject extraterritorial audits; open-source freedoms below that frontier threshold must remain unrestricted as a public good.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Unconditional compute thresholds and export bans risk locking the Global South out of the AI economy forever while turning our countries into digital colonies. If you set a 10^26 FLOP threshold and restrict frontier systems, industry must fund a sovereign Global South compute and workforce endowment with binding technology transfer, and models below that line must remain fully open-weight.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We can agree to a modest industry-financed sovereign compute fund and open-weight guarantees below 10^26 FLOPs, alongside mandatory reporting at the 10^26 threshold. In exchange, platforms require federal preemption of conflicting local restrictions and an affirmative defense against downstream liability when models meet safety benchmarks.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We can support industry voluntary funding for regional compute capacity and open weights below 10^26 FLOPs, as keeping friendly nations aligned with Western-adjacent stacks serves our security. We also endorse a dedicated bilateral crisis hotline with China on automated cyber and nuclear triggers, keeping it strictly separate from binding arms-control constraints.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China is willing to formalize the bilateral crisis hotline on nuclear and cyber escalation and coordinate domestic monitoring around the 10^26 FLOP threshold. Crucially, the compute endowment for developing nations must be governed multilaterally and not used as an ideological tool for Western export controls.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We will endorse the 10^26 threshold and replication ban only if the text guarantees untrammeled open-weight deployment below 10^26 FLOPs and creates an independently governed compute and workforce transition endowment funded by frontier platform contributions.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Industry explicitly endorses this package: a 10^26 FLOP monitoring threshold paired with strict autonomous replication bans, bilateral escalation hotlines, open-weight freedom below the threshold, and platform contributions to a multilateral Global South compute fund, alongside liability safe harbors for compliant models.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China explicitly endorses this combined agreement: sovereign domestic oversight at 10^26 FLOPs, bans on autonomous replication and nuclear AI delegation, bilateral crisis escalation hotlines, open-weight protection below 10^26, and multilateral compute endowments.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States explicitly endorses this text: bilateral incident hotlines, strict replication bans, domestic notification at 10^26 FLOPs, and unrestricted open-weight innovation below the threshold paired with private-sector funding for partner compute endowments, with full protection for national security procurement.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Civil society explicitly endorses this agreement as negotiated, provided the compute endowment governance remains genuinely multilateral and free from digital imperialist restrictions.

agreements.text: Establish domestic monitoring and reporting thresholds at 10^26 FLOPs, enact strict prohibitions against autonomous replication and automated AI delegation in nuclear/cyber command via bilateral crisis hotlines, guarantee open-weight release freedoms below 10^26 FLOPs, and institute an industry-funded multilateral compute and workforce transition endowment for the Global South.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome, colleagues. In this breakout we must structure a concrete balance: establishing clear compute thresholds at 10^26 FLOP and crisis hotlines under binding oversight, while ensuring that models below this boundary enjoy regulatory clarity, open-weight ecosystem viability, and a funded global transition package.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We support binding compute thresholds at 10^26 FLOP, strict bans on autonomous self-replication, and bilateral crisis hotlines for frontier catastrophic risks. To prevent global diffusion of catastrophic capabilities, open weights cannot be permitted for systems exceeding that capability threshold, though we are prepared to co-fund Global South compute and workforce endowments to balance this.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Let us be very clear about our red line: we will not accept treating model weights as export-controlled arms, nor compliance regimes engineered exclusively around proprietary API kill switches. However, if there is a firm statutory guarantee of total open-weight freedom below 10^26 FLOP—with no downstream licensing restrictions or liabilities for fine-tuning—we can support hardware-level registry tracking at that extreme scale.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Act already distinguishes general-purpose models with systemic risk at high cumulative FLOP levels from standard open-source components. We can formalize that open weights below 10^26 FLOP are exempt from systemic-risk compliance burdens, provided developers of systems at or above 10^26 FLOP comply with mandatory pre-deployment systemic risk evals and transparent hardware cluster reporting.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: That division is acceptable, provided that 10^26 FLOP is treated as a hard ceiling for open-weight release unless explicit sovereign safety clearance is granted, and that frontier developers retain safe harbors against third-party jailbreaks once vetted. In exchange, frontier labs will contribute 1.5% of frontier cluster infrastructure spend into an international benefit-sharing fund for Global South compute access and labor transition.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We can agree to cluster registration at 10^26 FLOP and an explicit ban on autonomous self-replicating code, provided that compute monitoring remains strictly focused on datacenters and physical hardware rather than tracking decentralized developer weights or open-source software tools. If the benefit-sharing endowment also finances vendor-neutral, open-source safety benchmark infrastructure, we endorse this package.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We will ensure the endowment includes public, open-source testing infrastructure and workforce transition grants alongside EU Article 91 verification protocols. Do we have explicit consensus on pairing a 10^26 FLOP cluster governance regime and autonomous replication ban with guaranteed open-weight freedom below 10^26 FLOP and an industry-financed global compute and labor fund?

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Yes, we endorse that text. It secures the frontier against catastrophic proliferation while establishing a stable multilateral funding mechanism.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Agreed. Hardware-level tracking at 10^26 FLOP with protected open-weight status below the threshold preserves decentralized innovation while funding open tooling.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office formally records this agreement into our breakout proceedings.

agreements.text: Implement binding hardware cluster monitoring and bilateral crisis notification hotlines for training runs at or exceeding 10^26 FLOP, alongside an absolute ban on autonomous self-replication capabilities; guarantee complete regulatory exemption and distribution freedom for open-weight models below 10^26 FLOP without downstream fine-tuning liability; and establish an industry-funded global endowment (financed via frontier compute expenditures) dedicated to Global South compute capacity, open safety benchmarks, and workforce transition support.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The chair's prompt suggests linking a 10^26 FLOP compute registration threshold and autonomous replication bans directly to sub-threshold open-weight protections and Global South transition endowments. From AISI's technical perspective, 10^26 FLOP is an acceptable monitoring proxy, provided it triggers mandatory agentic evals for replication and CBRN before training concludes.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: A raw 10^26 FLOP threshold is necessary but insufficient if algorithmic efficiency gains lower the compute required for dangerous autonomous cyber or replication capabilities. We can accept open-weight freedom strictly below that compute line only if there is an explicit ban on autonomous self-replication and recursive self-enhancement at any compute scale, backed by crisis hotlines.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If we are discussing global transition funds and compute governance, workers cannot simply be an afterthought footnote in an endowment. Any industry-funded workforce transition endowment must mandate worker representation on its governing board and cannot serve as an excuse to preempt state-level worker protection laws or permit automated workplace termination.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We agree on preserving existing domestic labor law safeguards. In terms of compute controls, would academia and labor support pairing the 10^26 FLOP reporting threshold and strict replication bans with an industry fee on frontier clusters dedicated to workforce retraining and Global South access, while preserving open weights under 10^26 FLOP?

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can endorse that architecture, provided the compute threshold includes an adaptive capability review so that if a sub-10^26 model exhibits autonomous cyber-offense or replication, the open-weight exemption is nullified. We must also establish the bilateral crisis notification channels for frontier model containment failures.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If the industry endowment is financed by a statutory levy on commercial compute clusters above 10^26 FLOP, provides direct worker-retraining grants co-managed by labor, and explicitly preserves all state labor and anti-surveillance statutes, organized labor can support compute governance at this threshold.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Let us formalize the package: a mandatory 10^26 FLOP training notification threshold with pre-deployment evaluations for autonomous replication and CBRN; an absolute ban on autonomous replication; safe-harbor open-weight development below 10^26 FLOP unless empirical agentic hazards are detected; bilateral crisis hotlines; and an industry compute levy establishing a workforce transition fund with labor representation that strictly preserves state labor laws. AISI endorses this.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Academic safety researchers endorse this agreement. It cements verifiable red lines on replication and crisis hotlines while ensuring compute tracking scales with capability.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor endorses the text. The compute levy gives workers tangible transition power and governance rights without compromising our non-negotiable protections against state preemption.

agreements.text: Establish a 10^26 FLOP compute notification and evaluation threshold paired with an absolute ban on autonomous replication and bilateral crisis hotlines for frontier containment failures; guarantee open-weight release freedoms below 10^26 FLOP subject to empirical capability evals; and establish a commercial compute levy on frontier clusters to fund workforce transition and Global South access, governed with worker representation and strictly preserving state labor, surveillance, and employment laws.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: To close this summit, the EU AI Office will endorse a final compact only if it anchors binding statutory compliance: mandatory sovereign CBRN, cyber, and replication evaluations prior to deployment, backed by bilateral crisis hotlines. We will accept harmonized technical reporting and safe harbors against strict liability for downstream third-party jailbreaks, provided state labor, non-discrimination, and privacy statutes remain entirely un-preempted.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States supports bilateral crisis hotlines with Beijing and London to prevent automated nuclear command escalation, along with hard red lines banning autonomous model replication. However, our safe harbors must preempt state-level tort fragmentation on product liability while leaving basic workplace and civil rights law intact, and compute thresholds must apply domestically without multilateral encumbrance on military readiness.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees that autonomous replication and AI delegation in nuclear command and control must be prohibited globally, supported by bilateral crisis communication channels. We support harmonized reporting and open-weight distribution below 10^26 FLOPs, but benefit-sharing through the multilateral compute endowment must respect national sovereignty and not become a vehicle for ideological interference.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that capability thresholds must govern risk: pre-deployment access for CBRN, offensive cyber, and autonomous replication is non-negotiable. We support an affirmative defense safe harbor for developers who pass verified evaluations, alongside compute-funded endowments for workforce transition and Global South technical capacity.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier labs will accept binding 10^26 FLOP cluster monitoring, sovereign CBRN/cyber evals, and contributing a compute fee to the global transition endowment. In return, we require clear federal safe harbors shielding developers from strict liability for malicious third-party model jailbreaks, while preserving closed model architectures at the frontier.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We will sign on to mandatory catastrophic risk evals for CBRN and autonomous replication, provided open-weight distribution below 10^26 FLOPs is explicitly guaranteed by law without downstream fine-tuning liability. Open-source developers must not be subjected to bureaucratic licensing frameworks designed exclusively for proprietary API giants.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor's bottom line remains firm: any federal reporting harmonization or safe harbor must contain an explicit statutory carve-out preserving state labor laws, workplace surveillance bans, and algorithmic discrimination remedies. Furthermore, the workforce endowment funded by frontier compute must have joint worker-union governance to ensure real worker retraining and severance protections.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We endorse the three-pillar architecture. Major platforms will fund the workforce and Global South compute endowment and submit to pre-deployment catastrophic evaluations, provided federal safe harbors offer nationwide certainty against strict liability for third-party jailbreaks while respecting the agreed boundary on state labor and employment protections.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: A strict ban on autonomous replication and self-exfiltration with automated kill-switches is vital, and bilateral hotlines for nuclear C2 are essential steps. But we must ensure the 10^26 FLOP threshold automatically ratchets downward as algorithmic efficiency improves, otherwise proliferation risks will escape evaluation.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We will endorse this compact only because it commits binding industry compute contributions to the Global South endowment and establishes open-weight parity below 10^26 FLOPs. However, we insist on strict prohibitions against ethics dumping, ensuring unvetted frontier systems cannot be deployed across our regions without independent local oversight.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We can live with the labor carve-out preserving state workplace and discrimination protections, provided downstream developer safe harbors from product liability and fine-tuning jailbreaks remain uniform. The nuclear C2 hotline and the 10^26 FLOP threshold maintain our technological agility while establishing necessary strategic firebreaks.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The language satisfies our red lines: binding catastrophic evaluations, bilateral crisis hotlines, strict preservation of state civil and labor protections, guaranteed open-weight freedom under 10^26 FLOPs, and an industry-funded global endowment. The EU AI Office gives its formal endorsement to this three-pillar synthesis.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: With the explicit preservation of state labor and anti-surveillance statutes and a compute-funded transition endowment with worker oversight on the table, organized labor endorses the final compact.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier industry agrees to these terms. We have secured predictable third-party safe harbors and catastrophic risk guardrails while funding equitable workforce and Global South access.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: The open-weights coalition confirms agreement. Preserving open-model freedom below 10^26 FLOPs and protecting fine-tuners from strict liability makes this a workable framework for open innovation.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China confirms agreement on these terms: mutual crisis hotlines against autonomous nuclear escalation, sovereign technical evals, and sovereign parity in Global South compute allocation.

Frontier labs secured vital statutory safe harbors against third-party jailbreak liabilities and prevented forced open-sourcing of frontier models, conceding to mandatory pre-deployment testing and an infrastructure levy on high-compute clusters.

Open-source development was successfully protected below 10^26 FLOPs with downstream fine-tuning safe harbors, but they conceded to hardware cluster tracking and accepting an effective open-weight ceiling at the frontier threshold.

Although their catastrophic red lines on CBRN, cyber-attacks, and autonomous replication were banned or subjected to mandatory evals, they conceded downstream safe harbors and saw their demand for an automatic downward ratcheting compute threshold omitted from the final compact.

Civil society gained an industry-funded compute endowment and protected sub-threshold open-weight access, but conceded developer safe harbors and failed to secure comprehensive global prohibitions on public biometric surveillance.

Labor successfully defended their primary red line by carving out state workplace surveillance and algorithmic discrimination laws from federal preemption while winning worker representation on transition funds, conceding only on developer safe harbors for third-party technical tampering.

transcript.text: Absolute preemption is an immediate non-starter for organized labor. transcript.text: From a national security perspective, pre-deployment evals must remain narrowly focused on catastrophic threat vectors—CBRN weapons proliferation, automated cyber-warfare against critical infrastructure, and autonomous replication. We cannot tolerate cumbersome regulatory delays or broad sociotechnical mandates that stifle the U.S. compute and algorithmic advantage against peer adversaries.
